screens.title: Why testing is essential: immutability and risk
screens.narratorSegment: Define the problem first: smart contracts are immutable once deployed, meaning the code you publish is the code that will run forever at that address unless you deploy a replacement and migrate state. This permanence raises the stakes: bugs that would be patched in a traditional web app can become irreversible losses on-chain. A concrete example is a function that incorrectly calculates balances: if users deposit funds and a logic bug allows withdrawals to fail or mis-route funds, those assets can be permanently inaccessible or stolen. A common misconception is that testnets or manual trials are sufficient; they are helpful, but only automated, repeatable tests give you a reliable safety net as code evolves. Automated unit tests check each piece of logic against expected behaviors, integration tests check interactions, and E2E tests confirm the full flow. The takeaway is simple: treat tests as your pre-flight checklist. Design tests to include both happy paths and failure conditions — zero values, reverts, unauthorized access, and maximum bounds — because those boundaries are precisely where immutable systems fail in irreversible ways. How will you change your development process now that bugs cannot be patched after deployment?

keyIdea.title: Immutability matters

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why testing is essential
Definition

Immutability and testing

Smart contracts cannot be changed once deployed to a chain. That permanence makes pre-deployment testing the only realistic way to prevent costly failures.

Concrete example
A deposit function that miscomputes balances could lock or mis-assign funds. Tests catch such logic errors before they reach a live chain.
Common misconception
Relying on manual checks or testnets alone is fragile. Automated tests ensure repeatable verification as code changes.
Key takeaway
Make automated tests part of every deployment pipeline; tests are your pre-flight checklist.
Analogy
Think of deploying a contract like launching a rocket. You would not launch without a pre-flight checklist that is performed automatically and consistently. Tests are that checklist for smart contracts.
Checkpoints to include in tests
  • Verify function outcomes for normal inputs and boundary values.
  • Assert that unauthorized actors cannot call protected functions.
  • Confirm reverts occur on invalid operations and that events emit expected data.
Mistake to avoid

Testing only the happy path. Always include failure and boundary tests.

screens.title: Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing test types helps you allocate effort where it matters. Unit tests focus on single functions or contract methods in isolation; their goal is to assert that a function produces the correct state changes and reverts for specific inputs. For example, a deposit function should update a user balance and revert when the amount is zero. Integration tests broaden the scope: they validate interactions between multiple contracts, such as a Vault calling an ERC-20 token’s transfer function and handling a revert from that call. Integration tests find issues that only appear when contracts interact. End-to-end tests cover the full system, potentially including a front-end interacting with deployed contracts on a test network or a local fork. E2E validates the user journey and uncovers UX, gas, or transaction sequencing issues. A common trap is trying to cover everything with unit tests; unit tests are necessary but not sufficient. The right strategy layers tests: many unit tests, focused integration tests for cross-contract flows, and selected E2E scenarios for critical user journeys. Which test type would you prioritize for a high-value funds flow in your protocol?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Unit / Integration / E2E

Test Types Compared

Choose the right test scope to catch the class of bug you care about.

Scope guide
Unit
Single function behavior
Fast, isolated tests that verify outputs and reverts for specific inputs. Example: deposit updates balance and reverts on zero.
Integration
Contract interactions
Tests multiple contracts working together. Example: Vault handling ERC-20 transferFrom reverts or approvals.
End-to-end
Full stack journey
Validate the complete user flow from UI actions to on-chain effects on a testnet or local fork.
Example scenario
A Vault contract accepts ERC-20 deposits. Unit tests verify Vault's accounting functions. Integration tests simulate a token transferFrom and a revert from the token contract. An E2E test simulates a user depositing via a front-end and confirms the final balance on the chain.
Pro tip

Write many fast unit tests, a few targeted integration tests, and only essential E2E scenarios to keep the suite maintainable.

Pitfall

Relying solely on E2E tests for correctness; E2E is slower and harder to debug for small logic errors.

screens.title: Unit test example: asserting a deposit function
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete unit test pattern for a deposit function. The goal of a unit test is to assert the function's intended state changes and reverts at the smallest scope. In plain terms, you set up a fresh contract instance, call deposit with a valid amount, then assert the caller's balance and the contract's total supply changed as expected. You also test a failure: calling deposit with zero should revert. This pair of tests—happy path and failure path—illustrates the value of unit tests. A common misconception is that unit tests verify gas costs or end-to-end behavior; they do not. Instead, they validate core logic quickly and deterministically. The concrete example on-screen shows a test structure you can adapt: setup, action, and assertions using matchers that confirm state and reverts. After writing such tests, you should notice faster debugging and clearer fault localization, because failing unit tests point to specific functions rather than large integration surfaces. How would you design additional edge cases for deposit in your contract? Unit test example: asserting a deposit function means write short, focused tests that check both expected state changes and expected failure conditions for each function.. In practical terms, a concrete unit test pattern and what it verifies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Unit test example
Code walkthrough

Testing deposit — structure

Follow the setup-action-assert pattern: deploy a fresh contract, execute the function, then assert state or revert reason.

describe('Deposit', function () {
  it('updates balance on valid deposit', async function () {
    // deploy, call deposit with a positive amount
    // assert user balance increased and total supply updated
  })

  it('reverts when amount is zero', async function () {
    // call deposit with zero and expect a revert
  })
})
What this checks
  • State changes: balances and totals are updated correctly.
  • Failure conditions: function reverts on invalid inputs like zero.
  • Isolation: unit test keeps external calls stubbed or mocked where possible.
Concrete example
If deposit incorrectly increments total supply, a unit test catches the mistaken variable update before any user sees a discrepancy. Tests act as precise alarms that point to the faulty line.
Key takeaway

Write a small happy-path test and a small failure-path test for every critical function.

Common mistake

Testing only the success case. Always include the expected revert or edge-case assertion.

screens.title: Integration testing: contracts working together
screens.narratorSegment: Integration tests evaluate how multiple contracts behave together. They answer questions like: does the Vault correctly call an ERC-20 token, handle approvals, and respond if the token reverts? A concrete scenario: your Vault contract calls transferFrom on an ERC-20 token. An integration test will deploy both contracts, set up approvals for the Vault, then attempt a deposit and assert the expected outcome. It will also simulate a token revert—perhaps by deploying a token stub that intentionally reverts on transfer—to ensure your Vault handles that gracefully. Integration tests uncover incorrect address passing, bad return value handling, and unexpected side effects that unit tests cannot. A common misconception is that integration tests are slow and provide low value; in reality, focused integration tests for critical multi-contract flows are high-value and should complement many fast unit tests. The practical rule: write integration tests for interactions that involve external contracts, asset movement, or cross-contract ownership changes. Integration testing: contracts working together means use integration tests to validate cross-contract calls, return handling, and side effects that only appear when contracts interact.. In practical terms, simulating contract interactions and failure modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Integration testing
Scenario

Vault and ERC-20 interaction

Integration tests deploy both contracts and simulate real interactions including approvals and transfer behavior.

Test steps
  1. Deploy token and Vault contracts.
  2. Mint or allocate tokens to a test account and approve the Vault.
  3. Call Vault.deposit and assert token transfer and Vault accounting.
  4. Simulate token revert to ensure Vault handles errors safely.
Why it matters
Integration tests catch issues like wrong address usage, missing approval flows, or unhandled revert return values that unit tests won’t show.
Example pitfall
If your Vault assumes transferFrom returns true but a token reverts instead, funds could be inconsistent. An integration test that forces a revert reveals this mismatch early.
Pro tip

Use small token stubs in integration tests to simulate both normal and failing token behavior.

screens.title: End-to-end testing: scope and limitations
screens.narratorSegment: End-to-end testing validates the complete user journey, from a simulated user action in a front-end to the resulting transactions on a test network or local fork. E2E tests are essential for high-level assurance that the system behaves as expected under realistic conditions. They check UI workflows, transaction ordering, gas behavior, and integration with off-chain components. However, E2E tests are slower, harder to debug, and less deterministic than unit tests. A practical approach is to reserve E2E tests for the most critical user journeys—such as deposits and withdrawals that move real value—and to rely on unit and integration tests for most logic verification. A common misconception is that E2E alone gives security; it does not. E2E complements deeper automated tests but cannot substitute for thorough unit coverage or contract-level integration tests. In practice, a small suite of targeted E2E scenarios, combined with many fast unit tests and several integration tests, yields reliable protection without overwhelming development velocity. End-to-end testing: scope and limitations means use e2e selectively for critical flows; they validate system behavior but are slower and less precise than unit tests.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › End-to-end testing

End-to-end scope

E2E tests check full flows and external integrations under realistic conditions. Use them for high-value flows and user journeys.

What E2E validates
  • Front-end to contract interaction and transaction flows.
  • Gas and ordering issues that only appear in full transactions.
  • Integration with off-chain services oracles, relayers, or wallets in end-to-end scenarios.
Limitations
E2E is slower, more brittle, and less diagnostic than unit tests. Use E2E sparingly and pair with strong unit/integration coverage.
Practical rule
Prioritize E2E for fund movement and critical UX flows; test logic primarily with unit and integration tests.
Example

An E2E deposit test signs a transaction via a wallet simulation, sends it to a forked network, and confirms the balance change on-chain.

Hardhat Network features

Hardhat provides a local network with instant mining, debugging traces, and optional forking for realistic tests against live state.

Instant mining
Transactions confirm immediately so tests run fast and deterministically.
Detailed traces
Hardhat surfaces stack traces and revert messages to speed debugging of failing tests.
Forking
You can replicate a mainnet or testnet state locally to validate contract behavior in real-world scenarios without spending real assets.
When to fork
Use forking when your contract interacts with existing mainnet contracts or when realistic state matters for correctness checks.
Key takeaway

screens.title: Testing checklist and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Before every deployment, run a short checklist that targets the most common sources of irreversible issues. Include: unit tests for every critical function including happy and failure paths; integration tests for cross-contract flows such as token transfers and approvals; and at least one end-to-end scenario for any user flow that moves assets. Pay special attention to edge cases: zero amounts, very large amounts, unauthorized access, and reentrancy possibilities. Beginners often underestimate edge cases and rely on manual testing or console logs. Automated, repeatable tests are the antidote. Another common pitfall is poor test coverage on critical financial logic. Aim for high coverage on core accounting and transfer functions. Finally, treat tests as living code: update tests when you change contract logic, and make passing tests part of your deployment gate. Use this checklist as your pre-flight routine so you don’t deploy fragile, unverified code to an immutable environment. fullNarratorScript:
Testing smart contracts is not optional; it is essential. Smart contracts are immutable once deployed, and that immutability means mistakes can lock funds, open security holes, or cause permanent failures. In this lesson you will learn the different testing scopes—unit tests that validate individual functions, integration tests that verify interactions between contracts, and end-to-end tests that exercise the full user journey. We will also introduce Hardhat and Waffle as the developer toolkit that makes local testing fast and repeatable. You will see how Hardhat’s local network mines transactions instantly, provides debugging traces, and can even fork a live chain for realistic state testing without spending real assets. Finally, you will follow a short hands-on setup: initialize a Hardhat project, inspect the generated contract and test folders, and run the sample test to confirm your environment is ready. By the end of the chapter you will understand why edge cases, failure modes, and reverts are as important to test as the happy path, and you will be equipped to start building a test suite that prevents costly, irreversible errors.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why testing smart contracts is non-negotiable, distinguish unit, integration and end-to-end tests, describe Hardhat’s role in a test workflow, and initialize a basic Hardhat project ready for tests. First, you will learn to articulate the risk that immutability creates and how tests act as a mitigation. Second, you will be able to pick the right test scope: unit tests for single functions, integration tests for contract-to-contract behavior, and E2E testing for user journeys. Third, you will understand Hardhat features such as its local network, instant mining, detailed traces, and the option to fork mainnet state for realistic tests without spending assets. Finally, you will run the Hardhat initialization command and confirm the generated contracts and test folders. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or verification milestone so you can measure competency. These skills matter because a missed edge case can cost real funds; testing is the primary tool to prevent that outcome.

This page maps each learning objective to a small, verifiable action. For explaining testing importance, practice by describing a consequence of immutability and how tests can mitigate it. For differentiating test types, create a one-paragraph mapping of three scenarios to unit, integration, or E2E testing. For understanding Hardhat, demonstrate the ability to describe instant mining and forking, and why those features remove friction from tests. For initializing a project, actually run the initialization command and inspect the created folders and sample test. These demonstration activities are intentionally modest: they are quick checks that confirm conceptual understanding and practical readiness. When you complete them, you will have both the vocabulary to explain testing risks and a working Hardhat project where you can run repeatable automated tests. This combination of explanation and hands-on verification is the most reliable way to move from theory to safe, test-driven development.

Define the problem first: smart contracts are immutable once deployed, meaning the code you publish is the code that will run forever at that address unless you deploy a replacement and migrate state. This permanence raises the stakes: bugs that would be patched in a traditional web app can become irreversible losses on-chain. A concrete example is a function that incorrectly calculates balances: if users deposit funds and a logic bug allows withdrawals to fail or mis-route funds, those assets can be permanently inaccessible or stolen. A common misconception is that testnets or manual trials are sufficient; they are helpful, but only automated, repeatable tests give you a reliable safety net as code evolves. Automated unit tests check each piece of logic against expected behaviors, integration tests check interactions, and E2E tests confirm the full flow. The takeaway is simple: treat tests as your pre-flight checklist. Design tests to include both happy paths and failure conditions — zero values, reverts, unauthorized access, and maximum bounds — because those boundaries are precisely where immutable systems fail in irreversible ways. How will you change your development process now that bugs cannot be patched after deployment?

Distinguishing test types helps you allocate effort where it matters. Unit tests focus on single functions or contract methods in isolation; their goal is to assert that a function produces the correct state changes and reverts for specific inputs. For example, a deposit function should update a user balance and revert when the amount is zero. Integration tests broaden the scope: they validate interactions between multiple contracts, such as a Vault calling an ERC-20 token’s transfer function and handling a revert from that call. Integration tests find issues that only appear when contracts interact. End-to-end tests cover the full system, potentially including a front-end interacting with deployed contracts on a test network or a local fork. E2E validates the user journey and uncovers UX, gas, or transaction sequencing issues. A common trap is trying to cover everything with unit tests; unit tests are necessary but not sufficient. The right strategy layers tests: many unit tests, focused integration tests for cross-contract flows, and selected E2E scenarios for critical user journeys. Which test type would you prioritize for a high-value funds flow in your protocol?

Let's walk through a concrete unit test pattern for a deposit function. The goal of a unit test is to assert the function's intended state changes and reverts at the smallest scope. In plain terms, you set up a fresh contract instance, call deposit with a valid amount, then assert the caller's balance and the contract's total supply changed as expected. You also test a failure: calling deposit with zero should revert. This pair of tests—happy path and failure path—illustrates the value of unit tests. A common misconception is that unit tests verify gas costs or end-to-end behavior; they do not. Instead, they validate core logic quickly and deterministically. The concrete example on-screen shows a test structure you can adapt: setup, action, and assertions using matchers that confirm state and reverts. After writing such tests, you should notice faster debugging and clearer fault localization, because failing unit tests point to specific functions rather than large integration surfaces. How would you design additional edge cases for deposit in your contract? Unit test example: asserting a deposit function means write short, focused tests that check both expected state changes and expected failure conditions for each function.. In practical terms, a concrete unit test pattern and what it verifies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integration tests evaluate how multiple contracts behave together. They answer questions like: does the Vault correctly call an ERC-20 token, handle approvals, and respond if the token reverts? A concrete scenario: your Vault contract calls transferFrom on an ERC-20 token. An integration test will deploy both contracts, set up approvals for the Vault, then attempt a deposit and assert the expected outcome. It will also simulate a token revert—perhaps by deploying a token stub that intentionally reverts on transfer—to ensure your Vault handles that gracefully. Integration tests uncover incorrect address passing, bad return value handling, and unexpected side effects that unit tests cannot. A common misconception is that integration tests are slow and provide low value; in reality, focused integration tests for critical multi-contract flows are high-value and should complement many fast unit tests. The practical rule: write integration tests for interactions that involve external contracts, asset movement, or cross-contract ownership changes. When a transaction reverts, look for the revert reason and the line in your contract that caused it. This diagnostic information is your primary feedback loop for fixing bugs. A concrete workflow is: run npx hardhat test, read the failing assertion and stack trace, open the contract at the referenced lines, add or fix assertions in tests to capture the intended behavior, and rerun the tests. A misconception is that failing tests are a waste; instead, treat failures as precise signals pointing to incorrect assumptions. Use the stack and revert traces to narrow the fix quickly. Before every deployment, run a short checklist that targets the most common sources of irreversible issues. Include: unit tests for every critical function including happy and failure paths; integration tests for cross-contract flows such as token transfers and approvals; and at least one end-to-end scenario for any user flow that moves assets. Pay special attention to edge cases: zero amounts, very large amounts, unauthorized access, and reentrancy possibilities. Beginners often underestimate edge cases and rely on manual testing or console logs. Automated, repeatable tests are the antidote. Another common pitfall is poor test coverage on critical financial logic. Aim for high coverage on core accounting and transfer functions. Finally, treat tests as living code: update tests when you change contract logic, and make passing tests part of your deployment gate. Use this checklist as your pre-flight routine so you don’t deploy fragile, unverified code to an immutable environment. These three concepts are foundational. Immutability explains why pre-deployment testing is critical — a deployed contract cannot be patched in place. Unit testing is the foundational layer: short, isolated tests that confirm function behavior and edge cases. Integration testing checks how contracts interact and reveals problems that only appear when contracts call one another. Keep these definitions in mind while writing tests and choose the right scope for each verification to reduce risk.
